messages.body_plain:
Dear Tomi,

There is no way to change the width and height of the dB scale except
using the layout arguments as you did. Sorry.

Changing the size of the different is not that trivial as there are
different conflicts between the functions called within the spectro()
function.
Anyway, here is a way, not very clean but it works ;-)

library(seewave)
data(tico)
par(cex.axis=1.5, cex.lab=1.5)
spectro(tico, f=22050, osc=TRUE, scalecexlab=1.5, cexlab=1.5, cexaxis=1.5)

Best

Jerome

messages.body_plain:
DiegoLlusia a �crit :
> I've found that oscillo () doesn't show the segments of silence
> preceding and following signal onset and offset. How could I graph the
> whole recording with segments of silence?
> Regards
> Diego
>
>
Dear Diego,

oscillo() usually takes into account silence (ie signal with 0 values).
For instance:
data(tico)
silence <- rep(0, 11025)
oscillo(c(tico, silence), f=22050)

Maybe is it the 0 grey line that add confusion, so try this:
oscillo(c(tico, silence), f=22050, coly0="transparent")

Regards,

Caroline

messages.subject: Errors with Wave-class objects returned from functions
messages.subject_clean: Errors with Wave-class objects returned from functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I'm new to seewave but so far I am very pleased with it's
abilities.

I have been stumbling on one major problem though.  I suspect as I
have not seen it reported anywhere I must be doing something wrong,
but even when I follow examples I get the following error every time I
try to use a Wave object returned from functions such as cutw():
"Warning message:
In writeWave(object, filename) :
  channels' data will be rounded to integers for writing the wave
file"

For context here is an excerpt from a session:
> song = readMP3("Desktop/SongSparrow.mp3")
> song

Wave Object
	Number of Samples:      68544
	Duration (seconds):     3.11
	Samplingrate (Hertz):   22050
	Channels (Mono/Stereo): Mono
	Bit (8/16/24/32):       16

> play(song)
> short = cutw(song,from=0,to=2,output="Wave")
> short

Wave Object
	Number of Samples:      44100
	Duration (seconds):     2
	Samplingrate (Hertz):   22050
	Channels (Mono/Stereo): Mono
	Bit (8/16/24/32):       16

> play(short)
Warning message:
In writeWave(object, filename) :
  channels' data will be rounded to integers for writing the wave file

Nothing plays.  I have found a work around by using the standard
output of the functions in a matrix object then passing that through
my own function to convert that back to a Wave.  This works, but there
are some quirks to it.  Right now my function 'W()' as seen below only
works on 16bit waves, I need to recode yet more conditional statements
to make it work with 8/24/etc.

> short = W(cutw(song,from=0,to=2),song)
> short

Wave Object
	Number of Samples:      44100
	Duration (seconds):     2
	Samplingrate (Hertz):   22050
	Channels (Mono/Stereo): Mono
	Bit (8/16/24/32):       16

> play(short)
>

Works this way.  For completeness here is the W() function:
# W() takes as arguments the matrix data as well as EITHER the
sampling rate and the bit rate
# OR a template wave object from which these values can be extracted.
W = function(input,f=0,bit=0){
        if (bit==0){
                template = f
                f = temp...@samp.rate
                bit = template@bit
        }
        input = round(32000*input)
        if (any(abs(input)>32767)){
                cat("Warning: input values greater than wave tolerance.
\n",
                        "--> Normalizing data...",sep="")
                if (max(input)>abs(min(input)))
                        normval = 32767/max(input)
                else
                        normval = 32767/abs(min(input))
                input = round(input * normval)
                cat(" Input data scaled by factor of
",normval,"\n",sep="")
        }
        return(Wave(left=input,samp.rate=f,bit=bit))
}

Does anyone know why I encounter this error if I do not use try to use
the wave output from functions such as cutw() rather than using my
function to build a Wave from the matrix output?

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Errors with Wave-class objects returned from functions
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Errors with Wave-class objects returned from functions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Actually, the output of cutw() is normalized between -1 et +1 even when output="Wave".

The play() function waits for a sound between -2^15 and 2^15 for 16 bits sounds

Use the function normalize() before to run play() to fix the bug.

song <- readMP3("Desktop/SongSparrow.mp3")
short <- cutw(song, from=0, to=2, output="Wave")
short <- normalize(short, unit="16")
play(short)

In the next version of seewave, everything should work properly.

Best regards,

Jerome

messages.subject: Problem with autoc
messages.body_plain:
I have a WAV file which contains three transient waveforms which have
a high harmonic content.  The harmonics are very visible in a
spectrogram.  I am trying to use autoc to detect the waveforms and
calculate the fundamental frequency of each.  Unfortunately, autoc
isn't returning the results I want.  When I use the parameter
"fmax=500", it appears that autoc is returning all fundamental
frequency estimates above 1000 Hz, not equal to or lower than 500 Hz
as I expect.  Is this a bug, or do I misunderstand something?  Thanks
in advance for your help.

I have posted my R script, graphical results, and the WAV file at
http://guaminsects.net/anr/content/problem-autoc

Thanks in advance for your help.

- Aubrey

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Problem with autoc
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The main problem with your sound is that it is very noisy. Whatever the
parameters you use, it will always be very difficult to catch the
fundamental frequency.

You should first isolate the buz you would like to analyse. Then try to
remove as much as noise as possible with fir(). Eventually, it seems
that using the function fund() instead of autoc() gives better results.
Here is an example:

 > s <- readWave("05-02_9_2_example.wav")
 > f <- s...@samp.rate
 > s1 <- cutw(s, from=9.5, to=9.8)
 > s1F <- fir(s1, f, from=300)
 > fund <- fund(s1F, f, ovlp=75, fmax=500, plot=FALSE)
 > spectro(s1F, f, collevels=seq(-84,0, 1), scale=FALSE, ovlp=75)
 > points(fund, pch=20)

Another solution could be to use a FFT. You compute a spectrum right in
the middle of you sound of interest and then you get the peaks values
with fpeaks(). You just need then to compute the difference between two
successive peaks to get an estimation of the fundamental:

 > res <- spec(s1F, f, at=0.12)
 > res2 <- fpeaks(res, amp=c(0.01,0.01))
 > res2[2,1]-res2[1,1]
   freq
0.1875

messages.body_plain:
-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----
Hash: SHA1

Jerome Sueur wrote:
> The last version of rgl is 0.91, compiled with R 2.10.1
> The version of rgl you use is 0.84, compiled with R 2.8.1
> See:  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rgl/index.html

OK I purged again rgl from synaptic, and the  I downloaded the 0.91
version and tried to install it. It failed again, it seems that the
problem is that the standard setup of Ubuntu Karmic misses some Open GL
library (in particular glu.h).

I installed libglu1-mesa-dev which has the  glu.hl and then I was able
to install rgl and seewave.

Now it works brilliant
Pietro
